input: When a pressure measurement is made, the reading that is obtained is never perfectly exact, and it is helpful to have a clear vocabulary for describing how far it might be from the true value. The absolute error is the size of the difference between the reading and the actual value, expressed in the same units as the measurement itself. The relative error, by contrast, expresses that difference as a proportion of the reading, often as a percentage. For example, consider a pressure reading of 261 units with a tolerance of 1% of reading; the absolute error is then 2.61 units. It is important to distinguish error from uncertainty, two terms that are often used interchangeably in everyday speech. Error attaches to a particular reading, whereas uncertainty describes the range within which the value is believed to lie, taking into account all of the influences on the measurement. Keeping these concepts separate helps to avoid confusion when measurement quality is being discussed or specified. In practice, the distinction matters whenever a specification is written or a result is reported. If a figure described as an error is in fact an uncertainty, a reader may try to check it against a single reading and find that it does not reconcile; conversely, if an uncertainty is reported as though it were an error, the measurement may appear better characterised than it really is in practice. Careful usage therefore protects both the writer and the reader of measurement results, and it costs nothing beyond the discipline of choosing the right term.
target: A pressure reading carries an error as well as a value, and this passage sets out the two forms the error takes. Absolute error is defined as the size of the difference between the reading and the value it stands for, stated in the units of the measurement. Relative error is defined as the absolute error divided by the reading, stated as a fraction or a percentage of the reading. Take a pressure reading of 261 units with a tolerance of 1% of reading. The tolerance fixes the absolute error at 2.61 units. The relative error is the tolerance itself, because the tolerance was stated as a percentage of the reading. Error is not uncertainty. Error is the difference attached to a single reading; uncertainty is the range within which the value is placed when the measurement is reported, and it gathers every contribution the measurement carries, not the tolerance alone. Merging the two terms hides which quantity a figure states. A figure labelled as an error can be checked against a single reading and its tolerance; a figure labelled as an uncertainty cannot be reduced to that check, because it rests on the whole measurement, and the passage keeps the two apart throughout. The worked figures show the distinction in use. A tolerance stated as a percentage of the reading gives the relative error directly, and the absolute error follows from the reading it qualifies: change the reading and the absolute error changes with it, while the relative error stays where the tolerance put it. Neither figure says how the reading was obtained, what instrument carried it, or what else bears on it; those matters belong to the uncertainty of the measurement, which is stated separately when it is stated at all. Keeping the vocabulary apart keeps each figure answerable to its own check: the error to the reading and its tolerance, the uncertainty to the measurement as a whole.
